title: Allergic reaction at a food festival
setting: Food festival. 28F ate a satay skewer, now flushed with widespread hives, lip swelling, a wheeze and feeling faint. Carries an adrenaline auto-injector.
verdictExplanation: Sudden onset hives with airway (lip swelling), breathing (wheeze) and circulation (faint, low BP) involvement after a known trigger. This is anaphylaxis: a life-threatening emergency. Sick, needs adrenaline now.

shared.airway: Lip and tongue swelling, voice changing

er.exposure: Widespread hives over torso and arms

history.history: Ate a peanut satay skewer 10 minutes ago

cfa.question: What is your immediate management?

options.text: Help her use her adrenaline auto-injector, call 999 and sit her up to ease breathing
Lay her flat and give a glass of water to dilute the allergen
Wait to see whether the hives settle before acting
Give her antihistamine tablets instead of adrenaline

cfa.explanation: Adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis: help her use her own auto-injector into the outer thigh and call 999 immediately. If breathing is the main problem, sitting up helps. Antihistamines do not treat the life-threatening features and must not delay adrenaline.

er.question: What is your immediate management?

options.text: Give IM adrenaline into the outer thigh, call 999, position for the worst symptom and give oxygen
Give oxygen and antihistamine and hold adrenaline unless she deteriorates
Lay her flat with legs raised and reassess in 10 minutes before treating
Encourage her to walk to the first aid tent for treatment

er.explanation: IM adrenaline into the outer thigh is the priority and must not be delayed. Call 999, give high-flow oxygen, and position by the worst symptom (sit up for breathing, lie flat with legs raised if faint/hypotensive). Walking or standing an anaphylaxis patient can cause fatal collapse.

evolvingStage.narrative: Five minutes after the first dose she is still wheezing, more breathless and increasingly drowsy. The ambulance is several minutes away.

followUp.question: There is no improvement after 5 minutes. What now?

options.text: Give a second adrenaline dose, lie her flat with legs raised and chase the ambulance
Wait for the first dose to work; a second dose is unsafe
Sit her fully upright and give a sugary drink
Stop treatment until the paramedics arrive

followUp.explanation: If there is no improvement after 5 minutes, a second dose of adrenaline is indicated. With hypotension and faintness, lie her flat and raise the legs to support circulation, and expedite the ambulance.

levelExplanation.cfa: Use a second auto-injector if one is available and 5 minutes have passed without improvement.

levelFlags.cfaNotes: Adrenaline first, fast. Position by symptom and never stand or walk the patient.
levelFlags.erNotes: Anticipate a biphasic reaction; all anaphylaxis patients need hospital assessment even if they improve.
